title: Three Commanders at Mu'tah
subtitle: The Martyrdom of Zayd, Ja'far, and Ibn Rawahah, and the Prophetic Revelation in Madinah
summary: At the plains of Mu'tah, three thousand believers faced the vast imperial armies of Byzantium in one of the fiercest engagements of early Islam. In strict accordance with the prophetic decree, Zayd ibn Harithah, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah successively held the sacred standard until each fell martyred in combat. Hundreds of miles away in Madinah, the Messenger of Allah miraculously narrated their heroic stand in real time with tear-filled eyes.

sections.text: Upon arriving at the village of Mu'tah, situated in the windswept southern highlands of Jordan, the Muslim force drew up their defensive lines against the armored Roman formations and their Arab auxiliary confederates. The contrast was staggering: three thousand lightly equipped desert warriors confronting tens of thousands of professional legionnaires armed with heavy shields, iron breastplates, and forest of spears. Despite the immense odds, the believers stood shoulder to shoulder, anchored by unshakable faith.

The battle commenced with devastating fury. As designated by the Prophet, Zayd ibn Harithah stepped forward with the white standard of Islam, plunging into the thickest ranks of the Roman infantry. Zayd fought with heroic ferocity, deflecting blows and inspiring the ranks, until the spears of the enemy pierced his body and he fell as the first martyr of the day, sealing a lifetime of devotion to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Before the banner could touch the dusty earth, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib sprang forward and seized the standard. Leaping down from his reddish-blonde horse and hobbling it to signal that there would be no retreat, Ja'far advanced deep into the enemy lines, holding the banner high with his right hand while reciting verses extolling the beauty and eternal coolness of Paradise. Classical historical chronicles describe how the enemy concentrated their assault upon the standard. When his right arm was severed by a Roman sword, Ja'far caught the banner with his left hand. When his left arm was likewise severed, he clasped the standard to his chest with his upper arms, refusing to let the banner of monotheism fall until he was struck down with dozens of frontal wounds.

The Prophet later declared to the companions in Madinah that in exchange for his two severed arms, Allah had gifted Ja'far two emerald wings in Paradise, with which he flies alongside the angels wherever he wills. Henceforth, he became known in Islamic history as 'Ja'far al-Tayyar' (Ja'far the Flyer) and 'Dhu al-Janahayn' (The One of Two Wings).
The Steely Resolution of Abdullah ibn Rawahah

With Ja'far's martyrdom, the standard fell once more, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah rushed forward to claim it. For a fleeting second, looking upon the severed limbs of his comrades and the sea of Roman steel, human nature flickered within his heart. Instantly catching himself, he chided his soul with memorable verses: 'O soul, I swore that you shall enter, whether willingly or reluctantly! If people scream and draw their swords, why do I see you shrinking from Paradise?'

Leaping into the fray, Ibn Rawahah fought with relentless courage until he was mortally wounded, joining his two beloved brothers in martyrdom. All three appointed commanders had fulfilled their trust to the utmost, holding the line with their blood and demonstrating an unyielding devotion that stunned the Roman commanders.

Hundreds of miles to the south, the believers gathered inside the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, entirely unaware of the dramatic battle unfolding in the Syrian desert. Suddenly, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ascended the pulpit, his face reflecting deep sorrow and divine vision. Through prophetic inspiration, the distant battlefield was unveiled before his eyes, and he began narrating the unfolding events in real time to the weeping congregation:

أَخَذَ الرَّايَةَ زَيْدٌ فَأُصِيبَ، ثُمَّ أَخَذَهَا جَعْفَرٌ فَأُصِيبَ، ثُمَّ أَخَذَهَا ابْنُ رَوَاحَةَ فَأُصِيبَ — وَعَيْنَاهُ تَذْرِفَانِ — حَتَّى أَخَذَ الرَّايَةَ سَيْفٌ مِنْ سُيُوفِ اللَّهِ، حَتَّى فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ
'Zayd took the banner and was struck down; then Ja'far took it and was struck down; then Ibn Rawahah took it and was struck down'—and his eyes were shedding tears—'until a sword among the swords of Allah took the banner, and Allah granted victory through him.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 4262)

This authentic report from Sahih al-Bukhari not only validated the ultimate sacrifice of the three leaders, but also heralded the emergence of Khalid ibn al-Walid under the eternal title of 'Sayfullah'—the Sword of Allah. The sacrifice of Mu'tah proved that the foundation of the Islamic state was built upon selfless devotion, moral integrity, and leaders who were the very first to lay down their lives for their faith.
